items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: on the floor sitting at his feet was Charlie Shavers, the great trumpet player and a terrific — what a great guy Charlie was. And Joe Bushkin.

ctx.x: Okay. Well I’m going to — in the time I have then I’m going to leapfrog ahead, but only a little bit. Because I wanted to ask you about young Dan goes to Harlem. And I had heard a radio interview that you did, about going up to Harlem and checking out the music and stuff. I wonder what — can you describe like what a night would be like?

Well this was not too terribly long after I came to New York and I had met this little underground trumpet player named Matt Lorber, nickname was “Face”; he knew everybody and everybody knew him, and also met a very hip young lady who was the first to take me to the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and that actually turned out to be a night when Dizzy’s big band was appearing there with Chano Pozo, so I got to see that, which was tremendous. The Apollo was — one thing of course — the Apollo was frequented to some extent…

going, but it wasn’t what it used to be. But there were little clubs and there was this wonderful trumpet player and singer named Hot Lips Page. Lips was my friend, Nat was a kind of protégé of Lips’. Lips was from Texas and he didn’t call him “Face” but he called him “Shorty” which was pronounced “Shouty” — that was his Texas accent. items.q: Then other people came. Joe Bushkin, the pianist, came and brought a beautiful long-stemmed rose...

ctx.x: Before we get into the Army, I think you should recount your first meeting with Louis Armstrong.

That was not long before. I’ve written about that, so I won’t go into too much detail, but it was a fascinating experience, because Louis was working with the All Stars at the Roxy. The Roxy was the biggest movie theater in New York aside from Radio City Music Hall. Radio City Music Hall is a movie theater, but it is really more than that. Roxy was enormous. I think it was built in the last years of the boom. When it opened, the Depression was already – the market had already crashed. It was a huge, huge place.

Jeann Failows had asked Nat and myself to meet her at the backstage entrance there. We were going to meet Louis. Nat had met him before, but I hadn’t. We went up. [?] was backstage. We went up. They had very nice backstage facilities. There was Louis’s dressing room. Knocked on the door. The person who opened it was June Clark. June Clark had been a famous trumpet player in the twenties in New York. He and the great trombonist Jimmy Harrison were a famous brass team. Harrison worked with Fletcher Henderson. June…
